MACHINE LEARNING / REGRESSION

RIDGE REGRESSION

Least squares with an L2 safety net — shrink coefficients to gain stability under multicollinearity.

SupervisedRegressionRegularized
Build intuitionSee the visual
Saved only in this browser

STAGE 1 OF 6

Understand

01 The Problem

An econometrician forecasts next quarter’s growth from dozens of correlated indicators: GDP, inflation, unemployment, interest rates. Plain regression will fit, but the coefficients fly apart — a tiny data change swings them by 100%. The problem is multicollinearity: features that move together make the least-squares solution numerically unstable.

02 Intuition

Ordinary least squares tries to explain every wiggle, even noise — so coefficients inflate to chase outliers. Ridge shrinks every coefficient toward zero (it never zeros them), damping the wobble. Raise \(\lambda\) and the fit grows calmer, at the price of a little bias. The bias–variance tradeoff made tangible.

Overview

03 Overview

Why It Matters

04 Why It Matters

Ridge regression trades a pinprick of bias for a huge drop in variance. When \(X^{\top}X\) is nearly singular, the ridge term \(\lambda I\) makes it invertible and the coefficients behave. It is the default fix whenever features outnumber samples or march in step.

STAGE 3 OF 6

Mathematics

07 The Equation

\[ \hat{\beta} = (X^{\top}X + \lambda I)^{-1}X^{\top}y \]
  • \(X\) \(n\times p\) design matrix of features
  • \(y\) vector of \(n\) observed targets
  • \(\lambda\) regularisation strength — 0 recovers OLS, ∞ shrinks everything to 0
  • \(I\) identity matrix; the L2 penalty added to the diagonal
Mathematical Foundation

08 Mathematical Foundation

The objective adds an L2 penalty: \(J_{Ridge}=\|y-X\beta\|^2+\lambda\|\beta\|^2\). Differentiating gives \((X^{\top}X+\lambda I)\beta=X^{\top}y\). The \(\lambda I\) diagonal stabilises the matrix: even if features are collinear, \(X^{\top}X+\lambda I\) stays invertible. Shrinkage is the price of stability.

STAGE 4 OF 6

Learn

09 How It Learns

  1. Standardise features so the penalty is fair to all.
  2. Add \(\lambda I\) to the Gram matrix \(X^{\top}X\).
  3. Solve \((X^{\top}X+\lambda I)\beta=X^{\top}y\).
  4. Tune \(\lambda\) by cross-validation — small is less biased, large is more stable.

STAGE 5 OF 6

Practice

11 Worked Example

Forecast growth from 4 collinear indicators; OLS gives \(\beta=(12,-8,9,-11)\) — signs flip on reordering. Ridge with \(\lambda=4\) gives \(\beta=(1.9,0.6,-0.4,0.3)\): stable, sensible, every coefficient positive-ish. A little bias bought a lot of trustworthiness.
